title: Sandhya: water for the rising sun
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hook: demons at sunrise, water in cupped hands, and whose light the Gayatri means
carry: at sandhya, water for the sun, light for the mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shvetaketu's salt, and why Hindus point to Brahman as tat: that, you are. Today, the word that says whose.

Phones come out at sunrise on any beach, and not everyone agrees on what they're photographing. Some see the sun. Some see what the sun stands for. Readers of the Gayatri have split the same way for a long time. Its second word is savitur, of Savitr. Is that the sun in the sky, or something the sun only hints at? The honest answer: inside the tradition, both readings have their defenders. Here are both, at their best.
screen: `SAVITUR: OF SAVITR.` → `THE SUN, OR BEHIND IT?`

segments.voice: First the grammar, briefly. The god's name is Savitr; savitur means of Savitr. The radiance is his. In the Rig Veda's hymns, Savitr rouses the day and sets the world moving. Now a story about why the Gayatri meets the sun. In the Vishnu Purana, demons called the Mandehas try to devour the sun every morning as it rises. And every morning, brahmins at prayer cup water in their hands, say the Gayatri over it and throw it toward the sun, and the water strikes the demons like thunderbolts. The sun comes up. That's one story behind sandhya, the prayer at the joining times of the day, dawn, noon and dusk, with an offering of water to the sun called arghya. You can still see it: someone at a river or on a balcony, palms full of water, facing east. So, view one: the Gayatri belongs to a real morning and a real sun, a body standing in the light. Its strength is the practice itself. View two: some teachers, reading the Upanishads, hear Savitr's radiance as an inner light too, the light by which the mind sees anything at all. Its strength: the verse asks for thoughts to be stirred, not crops to grow. Many families hold both: the water goes to the sun outside, and the prayer asks for the light inside. Savitur says whose the radiance is, and leaves the rest to the one praying.
screen: `SAVITUR: OF SAVITR.` · `THE MANDEHAS ATTACK THE DAWN.` · `SANDHYA: WATER FOR THE SUN.` · `VIEW ONE: THE REAL SUN. VIEW TWO: A LIGHT WITHIN.` · then, large: `WATER OUTSIDE, LIGHT INSIDE.`

segments.voice: If you keep sandhya, this is a fine moment for it, as you were taught. If not, turn your body toward the brightest direction near you, a window or a lamp, sit tall with your palms resting on your knees, and feel the light on your face for a few breaths. Then, still facing it, notice the seeing itself, the part of you that knows there's light.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: savitur, of Savitr, the god whose light Hindus greet with water at the joining times of the day.

howItsDone: In sandhya-vandana, many Hindus offer water (arghya) to the sun with the Gayatri at dawn, noon and dusk; the Vishnu Purana tells that this water drives off the Mandeha demons. Some teachers also explain Savitr's radiance as an inner light that wakes the mind. Both readings are taught.

what a scholar hears: savituh is a genitive; its final breath turns to r before the v of varenyam. readers since have heard Savitr as the sun and as an inner light, and the sandhya rite keeps the sun in view.
